anchors.paper_title: Annotating, Understanding, and Predicting Long-term Video Memorability
anchors.reason: Cohendet et al. describes the video memorability dataset that supplied the stimulus clips' annotations, not the Essex EEG recordings from 27 participants.

metadata.methods_description: EEG was recorded with a BioSemi ActiveTwo system with 64 electrodes placed according to the international 10-20 system, sampled at 2048 Hz. Participants viewed movie clips, judged recognition and memory for each, and then annotated the moments that prompted recognition via mouse click during a second viewing.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

citation_details.title: Topological Bifurcation of Pre-stimulus Cortical Field Dynamics Predicts Cognitive Performance
citation_details.author: Diego Cerda Seguel
citation_details.abstract: Topological Bifurcation of Pre-stimulus Cortical Field Dynamics Predicts Cognitive Performance Abstract / Description for Zenodo (Deposit Description)This manuscript presents a large-scale computational analysis of pre-stimulus cortical dynamics and their predictive capacity for cognitive performance across three independent domains: episodic memory, motor control (exoskeleton), and perceptual decision-making. Using high-performance computing infrastructure (Patagón HPC), three public EEG datasets (ds006142, ds007788, ds002680) were processed, harmonized under the BIDS-EEG standard, encompassing a total of 48 healthy subjects and 21,524 experimental trials. Spectral variance within the beta band (13–30 Hz) was quantified in a strictly bounded temporal window spanning from −500 ms to 0 ms relative to stimulus onset (β_std). Key findings: Episodic memory (ds006142): β_std predicts memory retrieval success with AUC = 0.569 (p < 0.0001, n = 6,094 trials). Motor control (ds007788): β_std correlates with kinematic latency in exoskeleton control tasks, revealing a topological bifurcation in the population: two stable and opposite phenotypic profiles — stabilization (β_std ↓ → better performance) and controlled activation (β_std ↑ → better performance). Perceptual decision-making (ds002680): β_std correlates with reaction times in rapid visual categorization (r = 0.054, p < 0.0001, n = 9,146 valid trials). Implications: These results extend the classical Bereitschaftspotential principle (Libet et al., 1983) to non-motor domains, demonstrating that pre-stimulus cortical preparation is a transversal and predictive phenomenon. The observed phenotypic heterogeneity suggests that cognitive performance optimization can be achieved through opposite strategies of spectral modulation, challenging post-stimulus neural decoding models and opening new directions for adaptive brain-computer interfaces.
